title: Mento Entrepreneurship Lab — 6 Weeks (V2)
subtitle: Notice → Investigate → Empathise → Build → Run → Scale
description: A 6-week deep dive for older students. Move from spotting problems to defending a values-based decision against an investor. Built around 7 connected games: a 5-room mystery, customer-discovery interviews, a story pivot, a season of running a business, and a high-stakes founder debate.
tagline: Customers describe symptoms. Founders find needs.

outline.title: Notice — The Entrepreneur's Eye
outline.summary: Spotting problems is the entrepreneur's superpower. Start with a 10-week problem-to-product simulation.

outline.title: Investigate — The Vanishing Customer
outline.summary: A 5-room mystery: Priya's chai stall is losing customers. The obvious villain is wrong. Find the real cause.

outline.title: Empathise — The Customer Interviews
outline.summary: Talk to 4 customer personas. Listen for what they need, not what they say. Pick what to build next.

outline.title: Build — The Great Pivot
outline.summary: Your first idea failed. Now what? Live a startup pivot moment.

outline.title: Run — The Lemonade Empire
outline.summary: A full season of running a business: cash, reputation, weather, and supply trade-offs.

outline.title: Scale — The Ten Crore Question + Founder's Journey
outline.summary: Defend your values against an investor. Then synthesise everything in a full lifecycle simulation.

weeks.title: Notice — The Entrepreneur's Eye
weeks.summary: Entrepreneurs see problems where others see frustration. Train your noticing muscle through a 10-week simulation.
weeks.homework_summary: Carry a 'noticing notebook' for the week. Write down 5 problems you spot — anywhere.

content.intro: Over the next 6 weeks you'll follow Priya — a 14-year-old chai-stall owner who grows her business into a 12-store chain. Every game, every lesson, builds on the last.
content.mento_says: Hi! I'm Mento. This module is connected — what you learn in Week 2 helps you in Week 6. Don't skip lessons.

pillars.title: NOTICE
pillars.body: Train the entrepreneur's eye. Spot real problems where most people see noise.

pillars.title: BUILD
pillars.body: Investigate, empathise, prototype. Turn a noticed problem into something useful.

pillars.title: SCALE
pillars.body: Run a real business. Hold your values when capital pushes against them.

founder_spotlight.name: Priya Iyer
founder_spotlight.story: Started at 14 with one stall and her father's recipe. Within 8 years she ran 12 stores — and was offered ₹10 crore to compromise the recipe. Every decision in this module is a decision she actually faced.

content.key_takeaway: Entrepreneurship isn't a job title. It's a way of looking at the world.
content.question: What's one problem you noticed this week — even a tiny one?

content.intro: Most people walk past problems. Entrepreneurs notice them. The skill isn't intelligence — it's attention.
content.rule: If you can't name a real problem, you don't have an idea — you have a wish.

examples.complaint: School lunch is always cold by lunchtime
examples.idea: Insulated tiffin liner sized for Indian lunchboxes
Pooled short-ride app for 1-2km college commutes
WhatsApp-based pill reminder a family member can set up

examples.complaint: Notes from coaching are illegible by exam time
examples.idea: Voice-to-summary tool that turns lecture audio into clean notes

myths.myth: You need a brilliant, original idea to start.
myths.reality: Most successful businesses solve a boring problem better than anyone else. Originality is overrated. Specificity wins.
Noticing is a trainable habit. The 'entrepreneurial eye' is built one notebook entry at a time.

myths.myth: Big problems are better than small ones.
myths.reality: Small, sharp, expensive problems for a specific group of people beat vague big-vision problems every time.

content.key_takeaway: Every complaint is a problem. Every problem is the seed of an idea. Most ideas die because no one wrote down the seed.

lessons.title: Simulation: From Problem to Product
lessons.game_purpose: Live 10 weeks of an entrepreneur's life — spotting problems and acting on them — in 30 minutes of game time.

content.prompt: In the simulation, which problem felt closest to something you've actually noticed in your own life? Why?

questions.question: What's the difference between an idea and a wish?
options: An idea has a customer; a wish has nobody.
An idea is bigger; a wish is smaller.
An idea is original; a wish is borrowed.
There is no difference.
questions.explanation: An idea names a real customer with a real problem. A wish is just 'wouldn't it be nice if...' — there's nobody specific on the other end.

questions.question: Which of these is the strongest entrepreneurial signal?
options: A friend says 'you should start a company'.
A stranger spends 20 minutes complaining about something specific.
You feel inspired after a YouTube video.
Your parents think you're talented.
questions.explanation: A stranger spending real time complaining about a specific thing is the strongest signal — it tells you the problem is real, painful, and unsolved. The other options are noise.

weeks.title: Investigate — The Vanishing Customer
weeks.summary: Priya's chai stall is losing customers. Five rooms. One Saturday afternoon. The obvious villain is wrong. Find the real cause.
weeks.homework_summary: Pick a small business near your home (a shop, a tiffin service, a tutor). Ask the owner: 'What changed in the last 3 months?' Listen carefully.

content.intro: When a business starts losing customers, founders almost always blame the wrong thing. The new competitor. The weather. Fashion changing. The truth is usually invisible — and inside the business, not outside it.
content.rule: A drop in customers is a SYMPTOM. The cause is somewhere else. Investigate everywhere — especially the places that 'couldn't possibly' be the cause.

cards.title: The Obvious Villain
cards.body: The new competitor across the street. Easy to blame — almost never the real cause. If a competitor could kill you, your loyalty wasn't real to begin with.

cards.title: Silent Supply Drift
cards.body: A vendor changes a sub-ingredient without telling you. Your product changes 2%. Customers feel it before you do.

cards.title: Founder Palate
cards.body: You taste your own product daily. Your tongue adapts. Customers, who try it once a week, notice changes you literally can't.

cards.title: Bad Metrics
cards.body: Revenue is a lagging indicator. By the time the chart drops, the cause is 30 days old. Track inputs (ingredient quality, wait times, repeat rate), not just outputs.

content.story_hook: Saturday afternoon. Five rooms. One missing customer base. The clock is ticking. You play Priya — and the obvious answer is wrong.
content.key_takeaway: Sales are an outcome. Whatever caused the drop, the data is there if you know where to look.

lessons.title: Mystery: The Vanishing Customer
lessons.game_purpose: Live one Saturday afternoon investigating Priya's chai-stall mystery. Five rooms. The real cause is hidden in plain sight.

content.intro: Six lessons every entrepreneur learns the hard way — you just lived all of them in 35 minutes:

cards.title: Symptom ≠ Cause
cards.body: The visible problem (sales dropping) is rarely where the cause lives. Look at the inputs, not just the outputs.

cards.title: Obvious villains lie
cards.body: The competitor across the street is rarely the reason. Real causes hide in unsexy places — your supply chain, your own taste buds.

cards.title: Founder blind spots
cards.body: When you taste your own product every day, your palate adapts faster than your customers' do. Trust the soft signal.

cards.title: Supply changes are silent
cards.body: Suppliers can change your product without telling you. Build the habit of asking: 'has anything in the supply chain changed?'

cards.title: Customers know but can't say
cards.body: Loyal customers feel small changes long before they can articulate them. Ask open questions, not yes/no.

cards.title: Repair > Replace
cards.body: When a supplier or partner makes a mistake, the first instinct is to fire them. The mature move is usually to rebuild the relationship with new agreements.

content.prompt: Think of a small business you know that's struggling — a tiffin service, a stationery shop, a tutor. What might be the REAL reason it's losing customers? Write your hypothesis. Then explain how you'd test it without asking the owner directly.

questions.question: Priya's regulars stopped coming. What was the real cause?
options: Brewverse Café opened next door.
Priya raised her prices.
Her milk supplier silently switched brands when AarogyaDairy went on strike.
Customers are working from home.
questions.explanation: The real cause was a supply-chain change — Krishna Mama switched to GoldenCow milk because AarogyaDairy went on strike. Same price. Slightly different taste. Loyal customers felt it within 21 days even though Priya didn't.

questions.question: Why did Priya herself not notice the change?
options: She doesn't drink chai.
She drinks her own chai every day — her palate had acclimatised.
She was on holiday.
She's a bad chai-maker.
questions.explanation: Founder blind spot. When you consume your own product daily, your palate drifts with it. Customers, who consume it less often, feel the change more sharply.

weeks.title: Empathise — The Customer Interviews
weeks.summary: Six months later, Priya wants to add ONE new menu item. She talks to 4 very different customers before deciding. So will you.
weeks.homework_summary: Pick someone in your life. Ask them ONE open question this week — something starting with 'what' or 'why', not 'do you'. Notice the difference.

content.intro: Closed questions ('Do you like X?') get yes-or-no answers and miss almost everything. Open questions ('What was the last time you tried Y?') reveal what people actually do.
content.rule: If your question can be answered in one word, you asked it wrong.

examples.idea: What was the last time you really enjoyed a chai — yours or anyone's?

examples.complaint: Would you pay more for cold brew?
examples.idea: Tell me about the last hot drink you bought — what made you pick it?

examples.complaint: Are you going to a competitor?
examples.idea: Walk me through your morning yesterday — when did you first feel hungry or thirsty?

tests.name: PAST
tests.question: Anchor the question in something they already did. Memory > opinion.

tests.name: STORY
tests.question: Ask 'walk me through…' or 'tell me about…' — invite a story, not an answer.

tests.name: SILENCE
tests.question: After they answer, count to 3 before you speak. The second sentence is usually the truth.

founder_spotlight.name: Brian Chesky
founder_spotlight.story: Before Airbnb worked, Brian and his co-founders flew to New York and stayed with their first 100 hosts. Not 'do you like the app?' — but 'show me how you list a room. What's confusing? What did you almost give up on?' That on-the-ground listening is what turned Airbnb from a failing site into a $100B company.
founder_spotlight.lesson: The interviews founders dread are the ones that will save the company.

content.key_takeaway: Customers describe symptoms. Founders find needs. The way you ask the question almost entirely determines the answer you'll get back.

lessons.title: Game: The Customer Interviews
lessons.game_purpose: Talk to four very different customers. Listen for what they actually need under what they say. Then decide what to add to the menu.

content.intro: Each persona told you something — but what they said was a clue, not the answer:

cards.title: Vikram
cards.body: Said 'I don't eat breakfast'. Real need: portable morning energy. (Fix: cold brew or quick energy bite, not a sit-down breakfast.)

cards.title: Lakshmi Auntie
cards.body: Said 'too sweet'. Real need: a low-sugar option that respects tradition. (Fix: unsweetened option, not a modern oat-milk pitch.)

cards.title: Rohit
cards.body: Said 'bored of maggi'. Real need: filling food after football. (Fix: samosa-chaat, not novelty.)

cards.title: Anjali
cards.body: Said 'just want chai'. Real need: a place to linger emotionally. (Fix: a corner bench — an experience, not a product.)

content.key_takeaway: The right answer for the menu is usually one item that solves multiple needs at once — not a separate item for each customer.

lessons.title: Your Stated Want vs Real Need

content.prompt: Think of the last time you complained to someone — about school, a friend, a sibling. What was your STATED complaint? What was the REAL need underneath it? (No one will see this except you.)

questions.question: Which question is most likely to reveal a customer's real need?
options: Do you like our chai?
Would you pay more for cold brew?
What did you love about Priya's chai — and has anything been different lately?
Are you going to Brewverse Café instead?
questions.explanation: Open + emotional + two-part. Closed questions ('do you...', 'would you...') get yes/no and miss everything. The right question invites someone to talk about what they LOVE and what's CHANGED — exactly where the truth lives.

questions.question: What does it mean when a customer says 'bored of maggi'?
options: They literally want something new just for novelty.
It might be a polite way of saying 'maggi doesn't fill me up anymore'.
They've moved on emotionally.
Maggi is bad.
questions.explanation: Especially for teenagers, 'bored' is often a polite cover for 'still hungry'. The right move is to ask one more question — 'when did you last eat?' — and let the truth surface.

weeks.title: Build — The Great Pivot
weeks.summary: Your first product idea has failed. Cash is running out. The team is restless. Pivoting is one of the hardest moves in business — and one of the most important.
weeks.homework_summary: Find one famous company that pivoted (Slack, Instagram, Twitch, Nintendo). What did they pivot FROM and TO?

content.intro: Almost every famous company you know pivoted at least once. Slack started as a video game. Instagram started as a check-in app. Pivoting is failure transformed into intelligence — IF you do it right.
content.rule: Pivots based on data work. Pivots based on panic don't.

stories.name: Slack
stories.moment: Was a multiplayer video game called Glitch. The game flopped. The internal chat tool the team built to coordinate was the only thing anyone wanted. They launched it as Slack. Now worth $27B.

stories.name: Instagram
stories.moment: Was Burbn — a check-in app with games and photos. Nobody used the check-ins. Everyone used the photo filters. They cut every other feature. Sold to Facebook for $1B 18 months later.

stories.name: Twitch
stories.moment: Was Justin.tv — a guy livestreaming his own life 24/7. The audience grew only when gamers started streaming themselves. They renamed, refocused, sold to Amazon for $970M.

stories.name: Nintendo
stories.moment: Started in 1889 making playing cards. Tried taxis, instant rice, love hotels — all failed. Pivoted to electronic toys in 1966. The rest is Mario.

cards.title: Customer Pivot
cards.body: Same product, different customer. Your tool is being used by a different group than you expected — go where the love is.

cards.title: Feature Pivot
cards.body: One feature is the product. Cut everything else. Instagram's filters; Slack's chat. The hard part is letting go of the rest.

cards.title: Business-Model Pivot
cards.body: Product works, but not at this price or this distribution. Move from B2C to B2B, free to paid, or vice versa.

cards.title: Engine Pivot
cards.body: Same goal, different mechanism. Search engine pivots from page-rank to AI. The 'why' stays; the 'how' changes.

content.key_takeaway: Pivot = keep ONE thing, change the rest. Usually the thing you keep is what your existing customers told you they actually loved.

lessons.title: Story Game: The Great Pivot
lessons.game_purpose: Live a startup pivot moment — your original product is dead, revenue is zero, the team is restless. What do you save? What do you cut?

content.prompt: In your pivot story, what did you choose to KEEP and what did you choose to CUT? Which decision was hardest? Why?

questions.question: What is a 'pivot' in entrepreneurship?
options: Closing the company down to start a new one.
Keeping ONE thing that's working and changing the rest.
Switching the company's name.
Hiring a new CEO.
questions.explanation: A pivot keeps the strongest signal (a customer segment, a feature people loved, a unique insight) and rebuilds everything else around it.

questions.question: When is a pivot most likely to succeed?
options: When the founder is panicking about money.
When the team votes for it.
When data from real customers points to a clear new direction.
When investors demand it.
questions.explanation: Data-driven pivots work because they're grounded in something real. Panic-driven pivots usually fail because the founder is reacting to fear, not insight.

weeks.title: Run — The Lemonade Empire
weeks.summary: Time to actually run a business. Cash, reputation, weather, supply trade-offs — across a full season. Make decisions every day; live with the consequences.
weeks.homework_summary: Track one of your own resources for a week (time, pocket money, energy). Notice what depletes you and what grows.

content.intro: Designing a business is fun. Running one is a grind. The skill is to make small smart decisions every single day — and to recover from the bad ones without losing your nerve.

pillars.title: CASH
pillars.body: How many days of runway do you have? Every decision touches this. Run out and the game ends.

pillars.title: REPUTATION
pillars.body: Slow to build, instant to break. Cutting one corner can erase six months of trust.

pillars.title: SUPPLY
pillars.body: Lemons go bad. Sugar runs out. You buy more than you need, you waste; less, you stockout.

pillars.title: WEATHER
pillars.body: The thing you can't control. The skill is preparing so it doesn't break you on a single bad day.

content.rule: Plan for the bad day. Then run the good ones with confidence.
content.story_hook: Grandmother's lemonade recipe. 500 Mento Coins. One full season ahead. Every morning a choice: lemons, sugar, signs, sleep. By summer's end you'll know if you can run, not just dream.
content.key_takeaway: Most businesses don't fail dramatically. They fail one tiny decision at a time.

lessons.title: Simulation: The Lemonade Empire
lessons.game_purpose: Inherit your grandmother's legendary lemonade recipe and 500 Mento Coins. Run a full season — cash, reputation, supply, weather. Live the trade-offs.

content.prompt: In the lemonade season, what was the hardest trade-off you faced? What did you give up to gain something else? In hindsight, would you make the same call?

questions.question: Which of these is the strongest signal of a healthy small business?
options: High revenue.
Returning customers and stable margins, even if revenue is modest.
A growing social media following.
A lot of one-time buyers.
questions.explanation: Returning customers + stable margins beats high revenue every time. Revenue without retention is a leaky bucket — you'll burn out trying to fill it.

weeks.title: Scale — The Ten Crore Question + Founder's Journey
weeks.summary: The capstone. First, defend a values-based decision against an AI investor. Then synthesise everything in a full lifecycle simulation.
weeks.homework_summary: Write your own founder values — three sentences, hand-written. The kind you'd hold up against ten crore rupees.

content.intro: Every founder eventually faces a moment where capital and values pull in opposite directions. The choice you make in that moment defines the next decade of your brand — and yourself.
content.rule: If you don't know your values BEFORE the moment arrives, you'll discover them by accident — usually after compromising them.

value_axes.title: Quality vs Margin
value_axes.body: The cheaper ingredient saves ₹3 per cup. Customers can't 'taste' it in a blind test. But over months, loyalty drifts. The Week 2 lesson at scale.

value_axes.title: Speed vs Sustainability
value_axes.body: The investor wants 100 stores in 18 months. You know your supply chain, your team, your training can absorb 30. Saying 'no' is the discipline.

value_axes.title: Founder Control vs Capital
value_axes.body: ₹10 crore at 30% equity sounds great until you realise the term sheet gives the investor veto over your sourcing decisions.

value_axes.title: Customer vs Investor
value_axes.body: Investors are paying customers for your equity. Real customers are paying customers for your product. When they conflict, who wins?

founder_spotlight.name: Yvon Chouinard
founder_spotlight.story: Refused to grow Patagonia faster than its values could absorb. Famously ran a Black Friday ad saying 'Don't Buy This Jacket'. In 2022, he gave the entire $3B company away to fight climate change. Investors had been pressuring him to IPO for 30 years. He never did.
founder_spotlight.lesson: The hardest 'no' to an investor is also the most valuable thing you'll ever say.

content.key_takeaway: Naming a value out loud — to a counterparty who's testing it — is harder than thinking it. That's the muscle this week trains.

lessons.title: Debate: The Ten Crore Question
lessons.game_purpose: An AI investor offers Priya ₹10 crore — IF she swaps fresh masala for a cheaper packaged blend. Defend your values across 5 rounds against rotating pressure tactics.

lessons.title: Capstone: Startup Founder's Journey
lessons.game_purpose: A full lifecycle simulation — spark, co-founder, pivot, fundraise, scale, exit. Bring everything you've learned in five weeks into one decision-rich session.

content.prompt: Write three sentences naming what you would NOT compromise on, even for ten crore rupees. Why those three? When would they be hardest to hold?

questions.question: An investor offers ₹10 crore for a 'minor' product change that would save costs. The blind taste-tests show customers can't tell the difference. What does the milk-supplier story from Week 2 tell you?
options: Take the deal — the data is unambiguous.
Customers feel small changes within weeks even when they can't articulate them in blind tests.
Negotiate a better price.
Counter-offer with a compromise.
questions.explanation: Blind tests measure single-cup preference, not loyalty drift. The milk-supplier mystery showed exactly how a 'minor' supply change destroyed Priya's stall in weeks even though no individual customer could articulate it. Apply the same lesson at scale.

questions.question: What is the strongest argument against accepting a 'partial compromise' (cheap blend in only the new stores)?
options: It's not enough money.
A two-tier product is brand suicide — within 6 months the cheaper stores poison the original ones too.
Investors will judge you.
It's confusing for the team.
questions.explanation: Partial-compromise feels reasonable but is actually the most dangerous form of compromise — it lets the cost-cutting brand poison the original within months. Either you protect the brand promise everywhere, or you abandon it everywhere.
